options: Evaluates a formula and replaces any error value (of any type) with a specified fallback
Automatically fixes the underlying cause of a formula error
Deletes the cell if it contains an error
Only works with the SUM function
questions.explain: IFERROR catches any error type — #N/A, #REF!, #VALUE!, #DIV/0!, #NAME? — and replaces it with whatever fallback value you specify.

questions.q: Why is catching every error type with IFERROR a real analyst mistake, according to this lesson?
options: It hides genuinely broken formulas (like #REF! from a deleted column) behind the same friendly fallback text used for an expected 'no match', so the actual bug never gets noticed or fixed
IFERROR is slower to calculate than other functions
IFERROR only works on the first row of a table
IFERROR cannot be combined with VLOOKUP
questions.explain: IFERROR can't tell an expected #N/A apart from a genuinely broken formula — both get replaced with the same fallback text, which means a real bug can hide indefinitely.

questions.q: What does IFNA do differently from IFERROR?
options: It catches only #N/A errors, letting every other error type display normally
It catches every error type except #N/A
It works identically to IFERROR in every case
It only works with text functions, not lookups
questions.explain: IFNA is narrower on purpose — it replaces only #N/A (an expected 'no match'), while letting other error types like #REF! or #VALUE! stay visible so they get fixed.

questions.q: According to this lesson's practical rule, when should you default to IFNA over IFERROR on a lookup?
options: By default — because 'no match found' and 'something is broken' are different problems that deserve different treatment
Never — IFERROR should always be used instead
Only when working with dates
Only in workbooks with fewer than 10 rows
questions.explain: The lesson recommends IFNA as the default for lookups specifically because it preserves the visibility of real errors while still cleanly handling the expected 'no match' case.

questions.q: What does the #N/A error from a lookup function typically mean?
options: No match was found — usually an expected, legitimate outcome for some rows
The workbook file is corrupted
The formula contains a syntax error
The formula reference points to a different workbook
questions.explain: #N/A specifically signals 'no match found', which is often a normal and expected result — unlike #REF!, #VALUE!, or #NAME?, which usually indicate something is actually broken.
